Prequestions did not slow reading of the relevant material overall: the Bayes factors favoured no difference in typical reading time (μ), both in first-pass reading and in total gaze duration. Instead, the additional processing appeared on a subset of encounters, as occasional unusually long readings (τ), and in returns to the answers. It was also confined to the prequestioned sentences, so prequestions changed how readers treated their answers, not how they read the passage. This fits the absence of both a general benefit and a general cost in the meta-analysis of @kingshepard2025, and it argues against accounts on which prequestions raise curiosity or monitoring for the topic as a whole.`r claim(BY_row("first_pass", "Prequestioned", par = "mu")$BF01 > 3 && BY_row("total_fix", "Prequestioned", par = "mu")$BF01 > 3, "Discussion: Bayes factors favour no difference in μ, in first-pass reading and total gaze duration")`

We suggest that this additional processing is triggered when a reader recognizes that a sentence answers one of the prequestions. @lewis2012 proposed a similar mechanism: a sentence that shares words and meaning with a prequestion "resonates" with the reader's memory of the question and prompts the reader to re-inspect it. Recognition can occur only once enough of a sentence has been read, and it can fail if the reader misses the connection or has forgotten the question, so it should lengthen some readings rather than shift all of them—an effect on τ but not μ. Unlike text degradation, which slows all fixations [@white2012], prequestions lengthened only a subset of readings, as familiarity does in scene viewing [@guy2020]. The longer tail in first-pass reading suggests that recognition often occurs as an answer is first read; the look-backs and longer re-reading suggest that readers then return to the answer, perhaps to compare it with the question or their earlier guess, or to rehearse it. Recognition may also be what makes prequestions effective: in video lectures, prequestions enhanced learning only when learners remembered them [@sthilaire2020]. The attentional-window account [@sana2023] explains the long readings—attention is heightened until an answer is found—but not the look-backs, because once an answer has been found attention should return to its usual level.

The results also add to evidence that attention is not the whole story. If prequestions simply heightened attention to the content they address, that content should have been read more slowly throughout, shifting μ. Instead, processing increased only on some encounters with an answer and in later returns to it, consistent with findings that prequestions can improve learning without increasing study time [@motz2026]. This sequence—recognition first, attention after—is what the mental model hypothesis predicts [@motz2026], although our non-prequestioned sentences, about the other disease, cannot show whether activated knowledge also helps related information on the prequestioned topic. The pauses and returns also resemble metacognitive monitoring, in which learners look for information that fills the gaps the prequestions revealed [@kingshepard2025]; recognizing an answer is itself a metacognitive judgment. Eye movements alone cannot separate these accounts, but combining them with direct measures of metacognition, such as judgments of learning [@kingshepard2025], could. Nor can these data show that the additional processing produces the memory benefit: reading was observed rather than manipulated, and prequestions may also strengthen memory in ways that leave little trace in reading time. Experiments that control whether readers can return to the answers could test this.

These findings agree with the two previous eye-tracking studies in showing that prequestions shift attention toward the information they address. Because our TB group read the same text as Experiment 2 of @lewis2012 after prequestions on the same topic, comparing it with the no-prequestion group on the TB material is close to a replication of that experiment (descriptive comparisons from the Group × Topic models). As in @lewis2012, TB prequestions improved memory for the TB information (`r tb_txt("final_test", "TB")`) and increased looking back to the TB sentences from later text (`r tb_txt("regressed_in", "TB")`) and the time spent re-reading them (`r tb_txt("reread_time", "TB")`). Unlike @lewis2012, who found more re-inspection of the targeted sentences during first-pass reading, we found no reliable difference in first-pass reading of the TB sentences (μ: `r tb_txt("first_pass", "TB")`; τ: `r tb_txt("first_pass", "TB", "tau")`). Pooled over both prequestion groups, however, selective regression-path duration showed a longer tail but no shift in typical reading time, although with weak evidence.`r claim(tb_row("final_test", "TB")$lo > 0 && tb_row("regressed_in", "TB")$lo > 0 && tb_row("reread_time", "TB")$lo > 0 && tb_row("first_pass", "TB")$lo < 0 && tb_row("first_pass", "TB", "tau")$lo < 0, "Discussion: comparison of the TB group with Lewis and Mensink (2012)")` Separating μ from τ was important here: an analysis of means, as in previous studies, would dilute effects confined to a subset of readings and could not distinguish them from slower reading overall. The studies also differ in design and measures: the present study compared every target sentence with and without prequestions in a larger sample, measured re-reading as time on the sentence itself after the reader had moved on, and measured first-pass reading as selective regression-path duration [@schotter2025], because about half of first passes were cut short by a brief return to the preceding line. @bostan2026 likewise found more fixations on prequestioned sentences and more transitions between them, paralleling our look-backs, but unlike most prequestion research they also found a general benefit. Their integrative prequestions required combining information across the text and may have directed attention to non-prequestioned information as well [@pan2023], whereas our prequestions about single facts did neither. With 12 participants per group, however, their estimates are imprecise.

Several limitations should be noted. Each topic was represented by only five target sentences and five test questions, and the Polio and TB sentences differed in length, content, reading level, and position on the page, so the within-group Polio − TB differences combine effects of prequestions with differences between the materials. We therefore based our conclusions on the pooled comparisons, which compare the same sentences and questions with and without prequestions, and treated the Group × Topic contrasts as converging evidence. The topics also differed in how strongly prequestions affected them: the increase in look-backs and re-reading came mainly from the TB group, whose target sentences were already looked back to more often without prequestions. Future studies should control target sentences more closely—matching them across topics in length, reading level, position on the page, and wording overlap with the questions [@lewis2012], or varying which sentences serve as targets across versions of the text—and use more of them. The comparisons with the no-prequestion condition are between participants and so less precise than within-reader comparisons. The Bayes factors depend on the priors: they show that the data are better described without a general effect than with one of the size the priors allow, not that a small general effect is impossible. Finally, eye movements were recorded without head stabilization, and vertical drift was corrected only within the calibration accuracy criterion.

In sum, prequestions guide where readers look, and only toward the information they target: rather than reading the relevant material more slowly, readers pause on some of the answers and return to them later, while reading the rest of the text as they would without prequestions. Prequestions therefore do not simply heighten attention to the material they address. Such recognition-triggered processing is a plausible route by which prequestions strengthen memory for their answers, but whether it accounts for the memory benefit remains to be tested.


# Questions and Scoring Rules {#apx-a}

Prequestion and final test responses were scored with the same rule-based script (`scoring_rubric.R`), written by Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic; model ID `claude-opus-5-5`) and applied identically to every response. Each question awarded one point per correct element present in the response (@tbl-questions, @tbl-scoring). Blank responses, "I don't know" and similar responses, and random keystrokes scored 0. Minor misspellings were accepted when the intended word was unambiguous (e.g., "afganistan"). The same rules were used for the prequestions and the final test.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-questions
#| tbl-cap: "Final Test Questions and Answers"
#| tbl-colwidths: [5, 8, 45, 34, 8]
#| apa-note: "Points = maximum points for the question. The Polio prequestion condition answered questions 1–4 and 10 before reading; the TB prequestion condition answered questions 5–9."
answer_key |>
  arrange(questnum) |>
  transmute(Q = questnum, Topic = Condition, Question, Answer, Points) |>
  knitr::kable(format = "pipe")
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-scoring
#| tbl-cap: "Scoring Rules and Agreement With the Second Rater for Each Question"
#| tbl-colwidths: [5, 63, 8, 12, 12]
#| apa-note: "One point was awarded for each credited element present in a response, up to the question's maximum (see Table A1). *n* = number of non-blank responses (prequestions and final test) scored by both the automated rubric and the second rater; Exact = percentage of responses given the same score; ICC = ICC(2,1), absolute agreement."
credited <- c(
  `1`  = "The number 17 (as a whole number, e.g., not 170).",
  `2`  = "A negative answer: \"no\", \"no cure\", or \"not a cure\".",
  `3`  = "One point each for Nigeria, India, Pakistan, and Afghanistan.",
  `4`  = "One point each for antibiotics; analgesics or pain relief; exercise (including physical activity or therapy); and diet or nutrition. \"Antibiotic resistance\" alone was not credited.",
  `5`  = "One point each for cough (or blood-tinged sputum/phlegm); fever (or temperature); sweats (including night sweats); and weight loss.",
  `6`  = "10% (or \"ten percent\", 1/10); not credited if stated as \"less than\" or \"under\" 10%.",
  `7`  = "One point each for antibiotics (or antibacterials); two (two drugs, courses, rounds, or types); and long-term (long, extended, prolonged, or months).",
  `8`  = "A negative answer (\"no\").",
  `9`  = "One point each for cough, sneeze, and spit (or saliva).",
  `10` = "One point each for a starting value of hundreds of thousands (100,000–999,999) and an end value of about a thousand (500–9,999, or \"a thousand\")."
)
tibble(Q = 1:10, `Credited elements` = credited[as.character(1:10)]) |>
  left_join(transmute(rater$by_question, Q = as.integer(questnum), `*n*` = n,
                      Exact = paste0(fmt_num(100 * exact, 1), "%"),
                      ICC = sub("^0", "", fmt_num(icc, 2))), by = "Q") |>
  knitr::kable(format = "pipe")
```

# Model Specifications {#apx-b}

```{r}
#| label: tbl-models
#| tbl-cap: "Bayesian Models: Families, Effects, and Priors"
#| tbl-colwidths: [20, 22, 30, 28]
#| apa-note: "Pooled models: Status (prequestioned, non-prequestioned, no-prequestion) + Topic; Group × Topic models: Group (Polio, TB, no-prequestion) × Topic. Status, Condition, and Topic were coded with equal-prior contrasts, so the prior on the coefficients is also the prior on every pairwise difference between conditions (on the link scale). Other priors: intercepts normal(−1.5, 1) on the log scale (Gamma models; about 0.2 s per word), normal(0, 1.5) on the log-odds scale, and normal(0.2, 0.2) s per word for μ; ex-Gaussian σ and τ intercepts normal(−2.5, 1) on the softplus scale; random-effect *SD*s Student-*t*(3, 0, *v*) with *v* = 0.5 (Gamma models, ex-Gaussian σ and τ), 1 (logistic and beta-binomial models), or 0.1 (ex-Gaussian μ); random-effect correlations LKJ(2); the Gamma shape gamma(2, 0.5); beta-binomial overdispersion exponential(0.1). Durations were modelled in s per word."
s_tab <- bayes$settings
tribble(
  ~Measure, ~Family, ~`Random effects`, ~`Prior on comparisons`,
  "Total gaze duration", "Ex-Gaussian (μ identity; σ, τ softplus)",
  "μ and τ: participants (intercept, Topic slope), sentences (intercept, Status or Group slope); σ: participants (intercept)",
  sprintf("μ: normal(0, %s) s/word; τ: normal(0, %s)", s_tab$s_mu, s_tab$s_log),
  "Selective regression-path duration", "Ex-Gaussian (μ identity; σ, τ softplus)",
  "μ and τ: participants (intercept, Topic slope), sentences (intercept, Status or Group slope); σ: participants (intercept)",
  sprintf("μ: normal(0, %s) s/word; τ: normal(0, %s)", s_tab$s_mu, s_tab$s_log),
  "Re-reading time", "Gamma (log)",
  "Participants (intercept, Topic slope), sentences (intercept, Status or Group slope)",
  sprintf("normal(0, %s)", s_tab$s_log),
  "Regression-in (look-back)", "Bernoulli (logit)", "Participants (intercept, Topic slope), sentences (intercept, Status or Group slope)",
  sprintf("normal(0, %s)", s_tab$s_logit),
  "Final test", "Beta-binomial (logit)", "Participants (intercept, Topic slope), questions (intercept, Status or Group slope)",
  sprintf("normal(0, %s)", s_tab$s_logit),
  "Prequestions", "Beta-binomial (logit)", "Participants (intercept), questions (intercept)",
  sprintf("normal(0, %s)", s_tab$s_logit)
) |>
  knitr::kable(format = "pipe")
```

# Drift Correction {#apx-d}

Each fixation was assigned to a text line after correcting for vertical drift, separately for each reader and page. The correction combines two approaches used in automated drift-correction algorithms [@carr2022]: assigning sequences of fixations to a line together, and modelling drift as a function of position on the page. First, a single vertical offset was estimated: candidate shifts of the recorded positions were tried in steps of 0.05 line spacings, and the shift that minimized the summed squared distance between each fixation and its nearest text line was kept (distances were capped at one line spacing, so that stray fixations in the margins had little influence). Second, consecutive fixations moving along a line were grouped into chains; a chain ended at a horizontal jump larger than 10% of the screen width (e.g., a return sweep to the next line) or a vertical jump larger than 0.6 line spacings. Each chain was assigned as a whole to the text line nearest its median position, so that a single fixation drifting toward a neighbouring line stayed on the line being read. Third, because drift often grew down the page or across it, a linear model of the recorded vertical position as a function of the assigned line's position and the fixation's horizontal position (recorded *y* = *a* + *b* × line *y* + *c* × *x*) was fitted to fixations whose chain lay within half a line spacing of its line; gaze positions were corrected by inverting this model and the chains were reassigned, and this was repeated five times. The linear model was used only if it was plausible (a vertical stretch within 20% and a tilt of less than one line across the screen); otherwise the single offset was kept. Throughout, the correction was limited everywhere on the page to the calibration accuracy criterion of 0.5° (`r num(max_shift_cm, 2)` cm, about 0.45 of a line spacing), so it could not move a reader's gaze by a whole line. Chains more than half a line spacing from every text line were treated as off the text.
